newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cannes to launch muted birthday edition.
newsitem.headline: Cannes to launch muted birthday edition.

text.p: The Cannes film festival launches its 50th birthday edition on Wednesday with celebrations slightly muted by reported Chinese censorship and by the stabbing of France's culture minister.
Organisers hastily amended the bill for the Golden Palm competition after Beijing, according to industry sources, banned Zhang Yimou's "Keep Cool", which had been picked for the May 7-18 jamboree.
There was no official explanation, but Chinese authorities have criticised previous films by Zhang for portraying China as backward in films for Western audiences.
Zhang's "To Live" won awards at Cannes in 1994 although he had been banned from attending.
"Destiny" by Egypt's Youssef Chahine, and "The Serpent's Kiss" by France's Philippe Rousselot were added to the selection only days before the festival started.
Entries will be shown before a jury headed by French actress Isabelle Adjani and including British director Mike Leigh and Zhang's favourite leading lady Gong Li.
The opening film "The Fifth Element" by Luc Besson, a violent science-fiction spectacular, will be unveiled out of competition on Wednesday in the absence of Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy.
Douste-Blazy was recovering after he was stabbed while campaigning in Lourdes on Friday for a parliamentary election.

"These days people want violence, blood, gore," Cannes supremo Gilles Jacob said only a week earlier of a competition which includes Wim Wenders' "The End of Violence" and Matthieu Kassovitz's "Assassin".
Actors Johnny Depp ("The Brave") and Gary Oldman ("Nil By Mouth") take a turn behind the camera for the first time.
American movies claim the biggest share of the selection with six entries including "Absolute Power" by Clint Eastwood and "L.A. Confidential" by Curtis Hanson, based on a novel by James Ellroy.

Organisers said the reclusive Ingmar Bergman was unlikely to attend a gala ceremony at which virtually all the surviving Golden Palm winners will award him a special Palm of Palms to mark the festival's anniversary.

Rubbing shoulders in a Cannes festooned with red and gold flags will be directors such as Michelangelo Antonioni, Robert Altman, Francesco Rosi, Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, Emir Kusturica, Constantin Costa-Gavras and Quentin Tarantino.

Stars will also flock to Cannes: Robert de Niro, Bruce Willis, John Travolta, Kim Basinger, Gina Lollobrigida, Catherine Deneuve, Hugh Grant and Victoria Abril among others. Michael Jackson unveils his latest record, and Christian Lacroix opens a boutique on the sea-front boulevard.

At midnight out-of-competition screenings, maverick American director Abel Ferrara will show "Blackout" in which model Claudia Schiffer makes her acting debut, and Britain's Kenneth Branagh will present his four-hour version of "Hamlet".

Candidates for this year's lucrative Golden Palm award include Italy's Francesco Rosi on a Nazi death camp survivor's odyssey through Europe ("The Truce") and Britain's Michael Winterbottom on a journalist adopting a child in Sarajevo ("Welcome to Sarajevo").
Outside the competition, Italy's Anna Maria Tato will show "I remember...", a moving documentary based on her interviews with her companion, the late actor Marcello Mastroianni.
